sections.content: You know *cuyo* from B1 Unit 5: "whose", agreeing with the thing owned, with no article after it. At C1 it is how an administration packs two facts into one sentence. *El ciudadano cuya solicitud fue denegada puede presentar un recurso* says who may appeal and why in one clause. The owner comes first (*el ciudadano*), then *cuya* agrees with *solicitud*, which is feminine singular. A report or a notice uses this pattern all the time, because the second clause stays short and the sentence needs no repeated *su*.

sections.title: Agree with the thing owned

the user whose deadline expires today
el usuario cuya solicitud fue denegada
the user whose application was denied
los usuarios cuyos documentos están en regla
the users whose documents are in order
las oficinas cuyas ventanillas cierran temprano

items.spanish: El usuario cuya solicitud fue denegada puede presentar un recurso.
items.english: The user whose application was denied may lodge an appeal.

items.spanish: El trámite cuyo plazo vence el lunes es gratuito.
items.english: The procedure whose deadline expires on Monday is free.

items.spanish: Los usuarios cuyas reclamaciones son aceptadas reciben una respuesta.
items.english: The users whose complaints are accepted receive an answer.

items.spanish: La oficina cuyo horario cambió atiende por la tarde.
items.english: The office whose hours changed serves people in the afternoon.

sections.content: English "whose" has one form, so nothing warns you about agreement. Look at the thing owned, not at the person: *el usuario cuya solicitud*, because *solicitud* is feminine. And do not replace *cuyo* with *que su*: *el usuario que su solicitud fue denegada* is a mistake, even though it sounds natural if you translate word for word.
